name: Non-Fungible Token
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: One of One: What Makes a Token Unique
lesson.summary: A non-fungible token, or NFT, represents a unique, individually identified asset rather than an interchangeable quantity, though what it actually guarantees is narrower than popular usage often suggests.
lesson.body:
Where a fungible token treats every unit as identical, a non-fungible token, commonly abbreviated NFT, does the opposite: each token carries its own distinct identifier, making it individually recognizable and specifically not interchangeable one-for-one with any other token in the same collection, even one issued by the same contract. Rather than tracking a single balance number per address, an NFT contract, following a standard such as Ethereum's ERC-721 or the more flexible ERC-1155, tracks ownership of specific, numbered tokens, recording exactly which address owns token number 7 as distinct from token number 8.

This traces directly back to the general concept of a token: an NFT is still, mechanically, just a smart contract's internal record of ownership, deployed on top of an existing blockchain and inheriting that chain's tamper-evident guarantees. What changes is the granularity of what gets tracked, an individual unique item rather than a fungible quantity, which makes NFTs suitable for representing things where identity genuinely matters: a specific piece of digital art, a particular seat at an event, a distinct in-game item, or a unique property deed.

Here a skeptical reader deserves a precise and important clarification, because popular discussion of NFTs frequently blurs it. What an NFT actually, verifiably guarantees is narrow: that a specific token, identified by number within a specific contract, is currently recorded as owned by a specific blockchain address. That is all the blockchain itself can attest to. The token commonly stores only an identifier and a pointer, often a web link, to whatever data it is meant to represent, such as an image file, and that underlying file is typically stored somewhere off the blockchain entirely, on ordinary web servers or decentralized storage systems that the blockchain has no control over.

This distinction has real consequences. Anyone can save, screenshot, or copy the image a well-known NFT points to, and doing so is not prevented by the blockchain in any way, because the blockchain was never protecting the image itself, only the ownership record of the token that references it. If the server hosting the linked image goes offline, the token can persist on-chain while the thing it was meant to represent effectively disappears. Owning an NFT also does not automatically transfer copyright or other legal rights to the underlying artwork unless a separate legal agreement explicitly grants them, a point that has caused genuine confusion and, at times, litigation.

None of this means NFTs lack legitimate uses. Verifiable, transferable proof of ownership for a unique digital item has real applications in ticketing, where a venue can confirm a ticket's authenticity and history without a centralized database, in tracking provenance for limited-edition digital or physical goods, and in representing ownership of unique in-game assets across compatible platforms. But the enormous speculative markets and inflated claims that surrounded NFTs during periods of peak public attention were built on a common conflation between what the technology narrowly guarantees, a specific ownership record, and what buyers often believed they were purchasing, which was frequently something considerably broader and less certain.
